deep.reconstruction:
The page contains no derivations. It is a list of research problems from Hilbert's notebook of problems and plans, each item separated by a rule. I restate each item below.

(1) End of an item begun on the previous folio. Its start is not on this page; the previous transcription ends with an unrelated geometry item, so a folio or line may be missing. The surviving text reads: '[...] must be possible, since in the cyclotomic field the theory of ideals can, as is well known, be based solely on the theory of higher congruences. Now try to shorten Kummer's proof by using only what is essential for the proof of Fermat's theorem.'
- Modern reading: in Q(zeta_p) the factorization of a rational prime q (q not equal to p) is read off from the factorization of the cyclotomic polynomial Phi_p(x) mod q (Kummer–Dedekind). So ideal theory there can be built from congruences modulo prime polynomials.
- Hilbert's plan is to streamline Kummer's proof of Fermat's Last Theorem for regular primes p, i.e. p not dividing the class number h(Q(zeta_p)). He wants to keep only what is needed: unique factorization into prime ideals, the p-th power argument for ideals, and Kummer's lemma on units.
- This was carried out in the Zahlbericht (1897), Part IV, on Kummer fields and regular cyclotomic fields, which ends with Kummer's Fermat theorem.

(2) 'Can the sequence of remarkable points of the Pascal hexagon (Pascal, Steiner, Kirkman [written 'Cirquemann'] points) be continued to infinity?'
- Setting: the hexagrammum mysticum. Six points on a conic give 60 Pascal lines, 6!/(2*6) = 60.
- These lines meet three by three in 20 Steiner points and in 60 Kirkman points.
- Further derived elements follow: 20 Cayley lines, 15 Plücker lines, 15 Salmon points, and so on.
- Hilbert asks whether this hierarchy of concurrences and collinearities continues without end.

(3) 'The Eulerian diophantine problem. See Legendre, Zahlentheorie [German translation by Maser, 1886], vol. 2, p. 140.' This is a bare reference. Which of Euler's problems is meant (for example, a quartic or square-sum problem) cannot be determined from the page.

(4) 'Geometric meaning of the division of the lemniscate arc into a+ib equal parts, and geometric construction of it if possible; cf. Jacobi, [Werke] vol. 6, p. 276.'
- Modern reading: complex multiplication of the lemniscatic function sl by Z[i]. Division by a Gaussian integer mu = a+bi means the values sl(k*omega/mu), which satisfy an algebraic equation of degree N(mu) = a^2+b^2 (roughly).
- Hilbert asks for a geometric interpretation of these points on the lemniscate, and for ruler-and-compass constructibility.
- By Abel (1827), the extension of Q(i) generated by these values is abelian of degree phi(mu) = #(Z[i]/mu)^*. Hence it is constructible iff phi(mu) is a power of 2 (my completion, not on the page).
- For a Gaussian prime of prime norm p, this is equivalent to p being a Fermat prime.

(5) 'Transfer Staude's thread construction of the ellipsoid into sphere geometry and line geometry, and see what corresponds there, in 4 or 5 dimensions, to Staude's 3-dimensional theorem on confocal quadrics.'
- Background: O. Staude, Math. Ann. 20 (1882), constructed the ellipsoid by a taut thread over a confocal ellipse and hyperbola.
- Hilbert wants images under Lie's line–sphere correspondence and in the higher-dimensional models of sphere and line geometry: the Lie quadric in P^5, and the Plücker/Klein quadric in P^5 (4-dimensional).

(6) 'Treat the field sqrt(a+bi), a, b rational integers, the same way as I treated the Dirichlet field, and derive the biquadratic reciprocity law; likewise the field cuberoot(alpha), alpha in the field of cube roots of unity, etc.'
- Modern reading: study the relative quadratic extension Q(i, sqrt(mu)) over Q(i), mu in Z[i], by Hilbert's genus/norm-residue methods. These were developed for the 'Dirichlet field' Q(i, sqrt(m)) in Hilbert, Math. Ann. 45 (1894).
- The aim is to obtain biquadratic reciprocity as a reciprocity/product formula for the quadratic residue symbol over Q(i) relative to that extension.
- Similarly, the Kummer extension Q(zeta_3, cuberoot(alpha)) should give cubic reciprocity.
- This is the program realised in the 1899 'Theorie des relativquadratischen Zahlkörpers' and in the Kummer-field part of the Zahlbericht (and later Furtwängler) for higher powers.
errors: No mathematical errors, since no derivations are given.
'Cirquemann'sche Punkte' is Hilbert's phonetic misspelling of Kirkman (Kirkman points).
Item (1) is a fragment: its beginning is not on the given previous page (folio 132 contains an unrelated geometry item), so the antecedent of 'muss/immer möglich sein' is lost.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a problem list. The number-theory items (shortening Kummer's FLT proof, relative quadratic and Kummer fields for higher reciprocity) are exactly the program Hilbert published in 1894–1899. The geometric items are standard 19th-century questions with no results recorded. The page documents planning, not new results.

checkable.asserts: Six points on a conic determine 60 distinct hexagons, hence 60 Pascal lines
Pascal lines meet three at a time in 20 Steiner points (each Steiner point lies on 3 Pascal lines)
Division of the lemniscate by 2+i (norm 5) has degree phi=4, a power of 2, hence constructible
Division by 3+2i (norm 13) has degree 12, not a power of 2, hence not constructible by ruler and compass
73 = 3^2 + 64*1^2, so 2 is a biquadratic residue mod 73 (Gauss's criterion, a consequence of biquadratic reciprocity)
17 is not of the form x^2 + 64y^2, and 2 is not a biquadratic residue mod 17

transcription_corrections: 'Cirquemann'sche' is as written by Hilbert; the intended name is Kirkman.
First word: the image reads approximately 'immer möglich sein' (a continuation fragment); the first word may also be 'muss'.
'höheren Congruenz' is probably 'höheren Congruenzen' (the ending is cramped at the margin).
'Jacobi Bd 6 S 276' is consistent with the image (Jacobi, Gesammelte Werke, vol. 6).
